ibkr.title: Interactive Brokers: automatic via Flex Query
ibkr.description: Nothing to install: tradenot.es fetches your executions from IBKR once a day and turns them into trades.
ibkr.step1: In the IBKR portal: Performance & Reports → Flex Queries → create a new Activity Flex Query.
ibkr.step2: Select the “Trades” section with “Executions” and all fields. Format XML, period “Last 30 Calendar Days”. Save it and note the query ID.
ibkr.step3: On the same page, open “Flex Web Service Configuration”, enable the service and generate a token.
ibkr.step4: Enter token and query ID here. The first fetch runs right away, then once a day.
ibkr.note: The token can only fetch reports: no orders, no access to your money. It expires after the period you chose at IBKR; then just enter a new one. Menu names in the IBKR portal may differ slightly. Paper accounts (DU…) are recognised as simulation automatically.

items.q: Is TradeNot.es really free?
items.a: Yes. There is no subscription, no premium tier and no credit card. Every feature on this page is free for everyone.

items.q: How do my NinjaTrader trades get into the journal?
items.a: Download the NinjaTrader add-on on the import page (your personal key is already inside) and import it once via Tools → Import → NinjaScript Add-On. From then on every fill is sent automatically, for all accounts, with partial fills, commissions and MFE/MAE.

items.q: Can I import trades from Interactive Brokers automatically?
items.a: Yes. Create a Flex Query at IBKR and enter token and query ID once. TradeNot.es then fetches your executions daily. The token can only read reports, it cannot place orders.

items.q: How do I import trades from TradingView?
items.a: TradingView has no interface for your own trades. Instead, export the order history from the trading panel as CSV and upload it on the import page. The format is detected and orders already imported are skipped.

items.q: Is the trading journal suitable for prop firm traders?
items.a: Yes. Trades can be analysed by account type (evaluation, funded, live, simulation), and NinjaTrader accounts from Apex, Topstep and other prop firms are recognised automatically. Daily limits for drawdown, trades and losing streaks help you stay within the prop firm's rules.

items.q: Can I share trades with my mentor?
items.a: Yes, with mentor mode. You create a link for a trade that only people with the link can see. The account name and your other trades stay private, and you can stop sharing at any time.

items.q: Where is my trading data stored?
items.a: On our own server in the Netherlands (EU). Your data is never sold or used for advertising.

rMultiple.definition: R-Multiple is a fundamental risk management metric that measures the ratio between profit/loss and initial risk. It normalizes every trade based on the risk taken, enabling fair comparison across different trades regardless of position size or absolute amounts. A positive R-Multiple shows a gain, a negative one shows a loss relative to risk.
rMultiple.formula:
R-Multiple = (Exit Price - Entry Price) / Initial Risk

For Short positions: R-Multiple = (Entry Price - Exit Price) / Initial Risk
rMultiple.example: Entry at $100, Stop-Loss at $95 ($5 risk = 1R), Exit at $110: R-Multiple = (110 - 100) / 5 = 2R (double the risk gained). Exit at $92.50: R-Multiple = (92.50 - 100) / 5 = -1.5R (1.5x risk lost)

initialRisk.definition: The amount of money you are willing to lose on a trade, calculated from entry price to stop loss price.
initialRisk.formula: Initial Risk = (Entry Price - Stop Loss Price) × Quantity

expectancy.definition: The average amount you can expect to win (or lose) per trade over time. It considers both win rate and average win/loss.
expectancy.formula: Expectancy = (Win Rate × Avg Win) - (Loss Rate × Avg Loss)
expectancy.example: 60% win rate, $150 avg win, $100 avg loss → Expectancy = $50

tradeRating.definition: A subjective rating (1-5 stars) reflecting trade execution quality. Considers factors like: following your plan, entry/exit timing, emotional control, and risk management. This helps identify well-executed trades regardless of P&L outcome.

winRate.definition: Percentage of trades that are profitable.
winRate.example: 60 wins out of 100 trades → Win Rate = 60%

winRateRiskReward.definition: Win Rate and Risk-Reward ratio (R-Multiple) are the two fundamental pillars of trading profitability. They are inversely related: the higher your average R-Multiple, the lower your win rate can be while remaining profitable. This is essential to understand, as many traders mistakenly focus only on high win rates. Momentum strategies often have only 30-40% win rate but are highly profitable through high R-Multiples (3R+). Mean-reversion strategies often have 60-70% win rate but lower R-Multiples (0.5-1.5R).
winRateRiskReward.example:
Scenario A (Momentum): 35% win rate, avg win 4R, avg loss 1R → Expectancy = (0.35 × 4R) - (0.65 × 1R) = 0.75R per trade (highly profitable).

Scenario B (Mean-Reversion): 65% win rate, avg win 0.8R, avg loss 1R → Expectancy = (0.65 × 0.8R) - (0.35 × 1R) = 0.17R per trade (profitable but less).

Scenario C (losing): 60% win rate, avg win 0.5R, avg loss 1R → Expectancy = (0.6 × 0.5R) - (0.4 × 1R) = -0.1R per trade (losing despite high win rate!).

Breakeven formula: With avg R-Multiple of X, you need minimum 1/(1+X) win rate. At 2R: 33.3%, at 1R: 50%, at 0.5R: 66.7%

profitFactor.definition: Ratio of gross profits to gross losses. Above 1.0 means profitable, above 2.0 is excellent.
profitFactor.formula: Profit Factor = Total Gross Profit / Total Gross Loss

riskReward.definition: Compares potential profit to potential loss before entering a trade.

maxDrawdown.definition: The largest peak-to-trough decline in account equity.

avgWinLoss.definition: Average profit of winning trades vs. average loss of losing trades.

pnl.definition: The net gain or loss from a trade after fees.

setup.definition: A specific pattern signaling a trading opportunity.

stopLoss.definition: Predetermined price level to exit and limit losses.
stopLoss.example: Long $50, stop at $48 limits risk to $2/share

equityCurve.definition: The Equity Curve is a graphical representation of the cumulative performance of your trading account over time. It shows the development of your capital from trade to trade and visualizes growth phases and drawdown periods. An ideal equity curve rises continuously with moderate declines. Analysis of the equity curve helps identify patterns: Is your performance consistent or dependent on a few big winners? Does the curve show long sideways phases or deep drawdowns? This is essential for psychological trading management.
equityCurve.example: Start with $10,000: After 5 trades (Wins: +$200, +$150, Losses: -$100, -$80, +$300) the equity curve shows: $10,000 → $10,200 → $10,350 → $10,250 → $10,170 → $10,470. The visualization immediately shows that despite 3 out of 5 winning trades (60% win rate), the largest win (+$300) was crucial. A flat or falling equity curve over an extended period signals the need for strategy adjustment.

consistencyTracker.definition: The Consistency Tracker is a visual heatmap of your daily trading activity over multiple weeks/months. Each tile represents a day: Green = profitable day, Red = losing day, Intensity = number of trades. This tool reveals patterns in your trading behavior: Are you trading too frequently? Are there day-of-week specific patterns? Are you consistently active or sporadic? Consistency is critical for statistically significant results. If you only make 5 trades per month, you need 100+ trades for valid strategy evaluation - that takes 20 months. More consistency = faster learning curve.
consistencyTracker.example: The heatmap shows: Monday-Wednesday mostly green with high intensity (many profitable trades), Thursday-Friday mixed or empty (less/no activity). This could mean: You perform better early in the week when the market establishes trends. Or: You become less disciplined towards the weekend. Analysis leads to adjustment: Focus on Monday-Wednesday trading, strict break Thursday-Friday → immediate performance improvement through elimination of weak days.

dailyTradeGoal.definition: The Daily Trade Goal is a risk management tool that defines two critical parameters: (1) A daily profit target in dollars and (2) a maximum number of trades per day. This feature helps you stay disciplined and avoid two common trading mistakes: Overtrading (too many trades from boredom or 'revenge trading' after losses) and lack of goal-setting (endless trading without clear exit criteria). Once you reach your daily goal OR exceed your trade limit, you should end the trading day. This promotes quality over quantity and protects against emotional decisions.
dailyTradeGoal.example: You set a Daily Goal of $500 with a maximum of 10 trades. Scenario 1: After 6 trades you have $520 profit → You stop for the day, take the profit, and avoid giving it back through overtrading. Scenario 2: After 10 trades you have $200 profit → You stop despite not reaching the goal because you've reached your trade limit. This prevents revenge trading or desperately chasing the goal. The system tracks your success rate: How often do you reach your goal? How often do you exceed the trade limit? This data reveals patterns and helps optimize your trading strategy.

breakout.definition: A breakout occurs when price breaks through a defined resistance or support level, signaling a potential new trend movement.
breakout.example: Stock trades at $45-50 for weeks. Break above $50 with high volume = bullish breakout

consolidation.definition: A sideways phase where price trades in a tight range, typically after a strong move. Shows balance between buyers and sellers.
consolidation.example: After 20% rally, stock trades in 5% range for 2 weeks – consolidation before next potential move

edge.definition: An edge is a statistical or informational advantage that increases your probability of winning beyond chance. Can come from strategy, timing, information, or execution.
edge.example: Your edge: Trading only specific chart patterns with 55% win rate and 2R avg win → positive expectancy

gap.definition: A gap occurs when opening price is significantly above or below previous closing price, often due to news during closed hours.
gap.example: Stock closes at $50, opens at $55 next day after positive earnings – $5 gap up

leverage.definition: Leverage allows controlling larger positions with borrowed capital than your actual capital permits. Amplifies both gains and losses proportionally.
leverage.formula:
Leverage Ratio = Position Value / Equity

Margin Required = Position Value / Leverage
leverage.example: $10,000 account, 2:1 leverage → can hold $20,000 position. 5% gain: $1,000 (10% on equity). 5% loss: -$1,000 (-10% on equity)

liquidity.definition: Liquidity measures how quickly and at what price an asset can be bought or sold without significantly affecting market price. High liquidity = tight spreads, fast execution.
liquidity.example: Apple (AAPL): Millions shares daily, $0.01 spread = highly liquid. Penny stock: 1000 shares/day, 5% spread = illiquid

positionSizing.definition: Position sizing defines how much capital to invest in a single trade based on risk, account size, and trade setup. Critical for long-term survival and growth.
positionSizing.formula:
Position Size = Risk Amount / Risk per Unit

Risk Amount = Account Size × Risk% (e.g., 1-2%)
positionSizing.example: $10,000 account, 2% risk ($200), entry $50, stop $47 ($3 risk): Position Size = $200 / $3 = 66 shares

scalping.definition: Scalping is a short-term trading strategy aiming to profit from small price movements through many daily trades (seconds to minutes holding period).
scalping.example: Buy at $50.10, sell at $50.20 for $0.10 profit × 1000 shares = $100. 50+ such trades daily

slippage.definition: Slippage is the difference between expected trade price and actual execution price. Occurs with market orders in fast/illiquid markets.
slippage.example: You want to buy at $50 (market order), but get filled at $50.15 = $0.15 slippage per share (0.3%)

supportResistance.definition: Support is a price level where buying pressure historically was strong enough to stop downtrends. Resistance is where selling pressure stops uptrends. Become self-fulfilling prophecies.
supportResistance.example: Stock falls to $45 three times and recovers = support at $45. Reaches $55 three times and falls = resistance at $55

takeProfit.definition: Take profit is a predefined exit point where you automatically realize gains. Should be based on technical analysis (resistance, Fibonacci, etc.) not greed.
takeProfit.example: Entry $50, take profit at $56 (previous resistance). With $3 stop = 2:1 risk-reward

trend.definition: A trend is the general direction of price movement over time. Uptrend = higher highs & lows, downtrend = lower highs & lows, sideways = no clear direction.

volatility.definition: Volatility measures the magnitude of price swings. High volatility = large price movements (high risk & opportunity), low volatility = small movements (low risk & opportunity).
volatility.example: Stock A: $50 ±$0.50/day (1% volatility), Stock B: $50 ±$2.50/day (5% volatility) = 5x more volatile

volume.definition: Volume measures the number of shares/contracts traded in a period. High volume confirms price moves (conviction), low volume = weak/questionable moves.
volume.example: Breakout above $50: With 10x normal volume = strong signal. With below-average volume = likely false breakout

mfe.definition: The highest unrealized profit a trade reaches before closing. Shows the best price level during the trade.
mfe.formula: MFE = Best Price during Trade - Entry Price (for Long)
mfe.example: You enter a long at $100. The price rises to $112 before falling back to $108, where you exit. MFE = $12 (or 12%).

mae.definition: The maximum unrealized loss a trade reaches before closing. Shows the worst price level during the trade.
mae.formula: MAE = Entry Price - Worst Price during Trade (for Long)
mae.example: You enter a long at $100. The price drops to $95 before rising to $108. MAE = $5 (or 5%).

glossary.subtitle: Essential trading terms and risk management concepts

revengeTrading.definition: Impulsive trading after losses with the goal of quickly recovering lost money. Often leads to larger losses through hasty, unplanned trades.
revengeTrading.example: After 3 losing trades you double your position size on the next trade to 'quickly' recover the loss.

fomo.definition: The fear of missing a profitable opportunity. Leads to hasty entries without a clear plan, often near the high of a move.
fomo.example: A stock rises 15% in one day. You jump in without analysis – and buy exactly at the day's high.

overtrading.definition: Making too many trades, often from boredom, impatience, or after losses. Leads to increased fees and worse average results.
overtrading.formula: Signs: Trades per day > planned maximum OR position sizes inconsistent
overtrading.example: Your plan allows 5 trades/day, but you make 15 because you want to 'do something'.

dayTrading.definition: Trading strategy where all positions are closed before market close. No overnight risk, but requires intensive market monitoring.
dayTrading.example: You buy at 10:00 AM and sell by 3:30 PM at the latest, never holding overnight.

swingTrading.definition: Positions are held for several days to weeks to capture larger price movements. Less time-intensive than day trading.
swingTrading.example: Buy on Monday after breakout, sell the following Friday when price target is reached.

momentumTrading.definition: Strategy that bets on strong price movements. 'Trend is your friend' – buy in rising, sell in falling markets.
momentumTrading.example: Stock breaks out of consolidation with high volume → Long entry to ride the move.

meanReversion.definition: Strategy based on the assumption that prices return to their average. Trading against extreme movements.
meanReversion.example: Stock falls 10% in one day without news → Buy expecting a recovery to the average.

marketOrder.definition: Order for immediate execution at the best available price. Guarantees execution, not price.
marketOrder.example: You want to buy immediately → Market Order. In high volatility, price may differ from expected (slippage).

limitOrder.definition: Order executed only at the specified price or better. Guarantees price, not execution.
limitOrder.example: Limit Buy at $50 means: Buy only if price ≤ $50. At $51, no execution.

trailingStop.definition: A dynamic stop-loss that follows price in the profit direction but stays fixed on pullbacks. Automatically secures running profits.
trailingStop.example: Long at $100, trailing stop $5. Price rises to $110 → Stop at $105. Price falls to $105 → Sell (instead of $95).

movingAverage.definition: Average price over a defined period, updated with each new data point. Smooths price movements and shows trends.
movingAverage.formula: SMA = Sum of Closing Prices / Number of Periods
movingAverage.example: 20-day MA: Average of last 20 closing prices. Price above MA = bullish, below MA = bearish.

candlestickPatterns.definition: Visual price patterns based on Japanese candlestick charts. Show the battle between buyers and sellers within a period.
candlestickPatterns.example: Hammer = small candle with long lower shadow at end of downtrend → possible reversal upward.

spread.definition: Difference between highest buy offer (Bid) and lowest sell offer (Ask). Trading costs incurred on every trade.
spread.example: Bid $49.95, Ask $50.05 → Spread = $0.10 (0.2%). With 1000 shares = $100 implicit cost.

bullBearMarket.definition: Bull Market = sustained rising prices (≥20% from low). Bear Market = sustained falling prices (≥20% from high). Defines market phase.
bullBearMarket.example: S&P 500 rises 30% over 12 months = Bull Market. Falls 25% = Bear Market.

correction.definition: Temporary decline of 10-20% in an uptrend. Healthy and normal, often offers buying opportunities.
correction.example: Stock rises from $100 to $150 (+50%), then falls to $135 (-10%) → Correction, not trend change.

riskSimulator.definition: An analysis tool that simulates various scenarios based on your historical trade data. Allows testing alternative strategies like different R-multiple exits, position sizes, or trade filters without risking real capital.
riskSimulator.formula: Monte Carlo: Random resampling of historical trades over 1000+ iterations to project possible future equity paths
riskSimulator.example: You test: 'What if I always exited at 2R?' The simulator calculates your hypothetical equity curve and shows whether this strategy would have been more profitable.

sections.title: Operator
No investment advice
sections.text: TradeNot.es is a tool for recording and reviewing your own trades. Nothing on this website is investment advice or a recommendation to buy or sell any financial instrument. Trading stocks, futures, options, currencies or crypto is risky and can lead to the total loss of the capital invested.

sections.title: Links to other websites
sections.text: The operators of external websites we link to are solely responsible for their content.

sections.title: Who is responsible
sections.text:
The controller for the processing of your data on tradenot.es is {{name}}, Netherlands, reachable at {{email}}.

TradeNot.es is a private, non-commercial project. We do not sell data, show ads or use any analytics or tracking services.

sections.title: What we store
sections.text:
- Account: email address, password (only as a hash, never in plain text) and, if you choose, first and last name. If you turn on two-factor login, also its secret key and backup codes.
- Login: while you are logged in, we store the IP address and browser identifier (user agent) with your session.
- Your trading data: trades, notes, journal entries, daily prep, settings, goals and uploaded screenshots. With automatic import, also the executions from your broker (e.g. account name, instrument, price, time, fees).
- Connections: your API key for the NinjaTrader add-on and, if you connect Interactive Brokers, your Flex token and query ID.
- Contact form: name, email address, subject and message. The message is forwarded to us by email and not stored in the database.

When you open the website, the server necessarily processes your IP address to deliver the pages. We keep no access logs or visitor statistics.

sections.title: Purpose and legal basis
sections.text:
We process this data only to provide the trading journal to you (Art. 6(1)(b) GDPR). Session data and the captcha on sign-up, password reset and the contact form protect against abuse (legitimate interest, Art. 6(1)(f) GDPR). We answer contact form requests on the basis of Art. 6(1)(b) or (f) GDPR.

The app's analyses, such as revenge trade detection, are visible only to you. They have no legal effect on you.

sections.title: Where the data is kept
sections.text: All data is stored on our own server in the Netherlands (Leaseweb data center in Amsterdam). Leaseweb acts as our processor for hosting. To send emails (confirmation, password reset, contact form) we use an email service provider as a processor. Your data is not transferred to countries outside the EU.

sections.title: Requests to other services
sections.text:
- Prices: when you pick a symbol in the trade dialog, our server looks up the current price at Yahoo Finance. Only the symbol is sent, no data about you.
- Interactive Brokers: once you set up the connection, our server uses your token to fetch your Flex reports from Interactive Brokers once a day and when you press the button.

The website loads no fonts, scripts or other content from third-party servers.

sections.title: Cookies and browser storage
sections.text: We set only one cookie: the session cookie for logging in. It is strictly necessary and therefore needs no consent. In your browser's storage (localStorage) we also remember the color theme. This setting never leaves your browser.

sections.title: Shared trades
sections.text: When you share a trade, anyone with the link can see that one trade: without the account name, and the note only if you include it. We count the views. Search engines do not index the page. You can stop sharing at any time.

sections.title: How long we keep data
sections.text:
Your data is kept until you delete it or delete your account. When you delete your account, we immediately remove all data including screenshots. Expired sessions are deleted automatically, as are accounts whose email address was not confirmed within 7 days.

For safety, we back up the database and screenshots daily on the same server. These backups are deleted after 14 days, so deleted data disappears from the backups no later than 14 days afterwards.

sections.title: Your rights
sections.text:
You have the right to access, rectification, erasure, restriction of processing, data portability and to object. Much of this you can do directly in the app: under “Account” you can export all your data as a ZIP file, reset your data and delete your account. For anything else, write to {{email}}.

You can also lodge a complaint with a data protection authority: in the Netherlands the Autoriteit Persoonsgegevens (autoriteitpersoonsgegevens.nl), or the authority in your country of residence.

sections.title: Security
sections.text: The connection is encrypted with HTTPS. Passwords are stored only as a hash, and you can secure your login with a second factor (authenticator app).

sections.title: Changes
sections.text: If the way we process data changes, we will update this policy. The date at the top shows the current version.

sections.title: What this is about
sections.text: TradeNot.es is a free trading journal, run by {{name}} as a private, non-commercial project. By signing up you accept these terms.

sections.title: Free of charge
sections.text: Using TradeNot.es is free. There are no paid features, no subscriptions and no ads.

sections.title: No investment advice
sections.text: TradeNot.es helps you record and review your own trades. The app gives no investment advice and no recommendations. You make your trading decisions yourself and at your own risk.

sections.title: Your account
sections.text: You need a valid email address. Keep your password secret. You must not misuse the service, for example through automated mass requests, attacks on the infrastructure or uploading unlawful content.

sections.title: Your data
sections.text: Your data belongs to you. You can export and delete it at any time. What we do with it is described in the privacy policy.

sections.title: Availability and liability
sections.text: We run TradeNot.es to the best of our knowledge but without any warranty. There may be outages, calculation errors or data loss, so export important data regularly. We are liable only for intent and gross negligence and for injury to life, body or health.

sections.title: Changes and termination
sections.text: We may change or discontinue the service. Before discontinuing it, we will inform you by email at least 30 days in advance so you can export your data. You can delete your account at any time. We may suspend accounts that misuse the service.

sections.title: Governing law
sections.text:
Dutch law applies. Mandatory consumer protection rules of your country of residence remain unaffected. If the language versions differ, the German version prevails.

Questions? Write to {{email}}.

items.q: How do I get started?
items.a: Sign up with your email address and confirm it via the link in the email. Then add trades with “Add trade” or import them on the import page.

items.q: What does TradeNot.es cost?
items.a: Nothing. There is no subscription, no premium tier and no advertising.

items.q: Which brokers and platforms are supported?
items.a:
- Automatically: NinjaTrader (via an add-on) and Interactive Brokers (daily fetch via Flex query).
- Via CSV file: the order history from TradingView and our own template, into which you can copy trades from any other platform.

Other CSV formats are not recognized.

items.q: How do I set up the NinjaTrader add-on?
items.a: Download the ZIP file on the import page; your personal key is already filled in. Import it in NinjaTrader via Tools → Import → NinjaScript Add-On and restart NinjaTrader. From then on the add-on sends every execution from all accounts. As soon as a position is flat again, it becomes a trade.

items.q: How do I connect Interactive Brokers?
items.a: In the IBKR portal, create an Activity Flex Query (Trades → Executions, XML format, last 30 calendar days) and enable the Flex Web Service to get a token. Enter the token and query ID on the import page. TradeNot.es then fetches your executions once a day, or immediately with “Fetch now”. The token can only read reports, not place orders.

items.q: Can I export or delete my data?
items.a: Yes. Under “Account” you can download all your data as a ZIP file, including a CSV file that can be imported again and all screenshots. There you can also reset all trading data or delete your account.

items.q: Who can see my trades?
items.a: Only you. You can share single trades via a link (mentor mode) and stop sharing at any time. The data is stored on our own server in the Netherlands and is neither sold nor used for advertising.

items.q: How do I keep sim, prop firm and live accounts apart?
items.a: Every trade has an account type (simulation, evaluation, funded, live); imported trades also carry the account name. Under Reports → Accounts you analyze the account types separately.

items.q: How do I create setups?
items.a: Under Settings → Trading setups you create your setups, optionally with a checklist. In the trade dialog you pick the setup and tick which criteria were met. Reports → Rule adherence then shows your results with and without the rules followed.

items.q: What are the journal and daily prep for?
items.a: In the journal you write notes about your trading days. In the daily prep you record your market outlook, key levels, your plan and your state of mind before trading.

items.q: What do win rate, profit factor, R-multiple and drawdown mean?
items.a:
- Win rate: share of winners among all trades.
- Profit factor: total gains divided by total losses. Above 1 you are profitable.
- R-multiple: result relative to the initial risk. 2R means you won twice what you risked.
- Max drawdown: largest decline from a previous peak.

The glossary in the dashboard explains more terms.

items.q: Is there a mobile app?
items.a: No separate app, but TradeNot.es works in the browser on phones and tablets.

items.q: Is TradeNot.es investment advice?
items.a: No. TradeNot.es only analyzes your own trades and gives no recommendations.

digital.question: Digital or on paper?
digital.answer: A digital journal like TradeNotes offers automatic calculations, visual charts, search functions, and can never be lost. The time savings compared to paper are enormous.

time.question: How much time does journaling take?
time.answer: With TradeNotes, documenting a trade takes less than 2 minutes. The weekly review takes about 15-30 minutes – time that pays off many times over through better trades.

beginners.question: Useful for beginners too?
beginners.answer: A journal is especially essential for beginners! The earlier you start documenting, the faster you'll recognize your strengths and weaknesses and avoid expensive beginner mistakes.

review.question: How often should I review my journal?
review.answer: Recommended: Short daily review after the trading day, thorough weekly analysis on the weekend, and a comprehensive monthly review.
